script.text: Drones flew at Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery. So why did oil prices jump?

Yemen's Houthis say they hit Ras Tanura on Wednesday, the kingdom's largest refinery, and set it on fire. The Saudi-led coalition says its air defences destroyed four drones over the site, with no injuries. It did not say whether the refinery was hit.

Satellite images from NASA and Planet Labs showed thick black smoke over the site, reports say. Aramco did not comment. Brent crude rose more than two percent at one point. The Houthis call it revenge for deadly Saudi strikes in Yemen.

The same day, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two more oil tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire. That claim is unconfirmed. Iran's military now warns ships to coordinate their passage with its forces.
Will the Houthis strike Saudi oil again this year? Yes or no?

upload.title: Houthis Say They Hit Saudi Arabia's Biggest Refinery #shorts
upload.description:
On Wednesday, November 25, 2026, Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery in the Eastern Province, the kingdom's largest (capacity about 550,000 barrels per day). Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree called the strike accurate and direct and said it caused fires; the Houthis also claimed attacks on Riyadh's financial district and described the operations as retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen that they say killed civilians. The Saudi-led coalition said its air defences intercepted and destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura (seven in the Eastern Province in total, per some reports), with no injuries from falling debris in an initial assessment; it did not say whether the refinery was struck. Saudi Aramco and the Saudi government did not respond to requests for comment (Reuters). Satellite imagery from NASA and Planet Labs, as reported, showed thick black smoke over the site. The extent of any damage has not been independently established. Brent crude rose more than 2% intraday (about $93.60, +2.41% at 10:16 a.m. ET, per OilPrice.com); reports differ on how it closed. The same day, Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said, via state media, that two oil tankers hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire, saying they had used an unauthorised route; this has not been independently confirmed and reports differ on the number of vessels. An Iranian military spokesperson warned ships to coordinate passage with Iranian forces. Tehran says normal shipping will not resume until its demands are met, including lifting the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports. Locations on the map are approximate; the line from Yemen shows direction, not a flight path.
